Operator:
Good morning, and welcome to the Aether Dynamics Q3 2024 Earnings Conference Call. All participants are currently in a listen-only mode. After the speakers’ presentation, there will be a question and answer session. To ask a question, you will need to register by pressing star one one on your telephone keypad. As a reminder, this conference call is being recorded.

I would now like to turn the conference over to Alex Rivera, Head of Investor Relations. Please go ahead.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you, operator, and good morning, everyone. Welcome to Aether Dynamics's Q3 2024 earnings call. Joining me today are James Harlan, CEO; Sarah Kline, CFO; Maria Gonzalez, Chief Manufacturing Officer; Dr. Raj Patel, Chief Technology Officer; Tom Reilly, Chief Supply Chain Officer; and other members of our leadership team.

Before we begin, I would like to remind you that today's discussion may contain forward-looking statements that are subject to risks and uncertainties. Actual results may differ materially from those expressed or implied by these statements. Please refer to our SEC filings for a complete discussion of these risks.

Now, I'd like to turn the call over to James Harlan.

James Harlan:
Thank you, Alex, and good morning, everyone. Thank you for joining us today. Q3 2024 marked a period of significant advancement for Aether Dynamics, as we continued to execute our strategic plan. Key achievements included substantial electric vehicle range improvements and efficiency gains across our lineup, successful cost reduction initiatives that lowered COGS meaningfully, gross margin expansion to new highs through scale and mix, record production volumes with high capacity utilization, proactive updates on supply chain constraints with effective mitigations, confident revenue guidance reflecting our momentum, and detailed delivery volume guidance by model positioning us for accelerated growth. The launch of our Aether X SUV has been incredibly successful, and we are seeing a very positive impact of enhanced brand perception and market share gains on our positioning in the premium EV segment.

Now, I'll turn the call over to Sarah Kline to discuss our financial performance in more detail.

Sarah Kline:
Thank you, James. Good morning, everyone. For Q3 2024, our revenue was $14.2 billion, representing a substantial 35% increase year-over-year. Our gross margin reached 23.8%, driven by increased production efficiencies, favorable product mix, and battery cost deflation. Operating expenses totaled $2.1 billion, and net income amounted to $850 million. We are in a strong financial position with $8.5 billion in cash reserves. We project $16.5 billion to $17.5 billion in revenue for Q4, with full-year 2025 guidance at $125 billion to $135 billion.

Let me expand on our gross margin performance first, which continues to be a key highlight of our Q3 results and a testament to the execution of our cost-down initiatives amid a dynamic EV market landscape. For the quarter, our consolidated gross margin expanded to 23.8%, up 450 basis points year-over-year from 19.3% and 210 basis points sequentially from Q2's 21.7%. This marks our sixth consecutive quarter of gross margin expansion, driven by a combination of volume scale, structural cost reductions, and an improving product mix.

In our automotive segment, which represents over 95% of revenue, excluding regulatory credits, our automotive gross margin reached 21.2%—a robust 520 basis point improvement year-over-year and 180 basis points quarter-over-quarter. Regulatory credits contributed an additional $185 million, or 260 basis points to the overall margin, primarily from ZEV credits sold to legacy OEMs like Stellantis and Volkswagen Group in Europe and California Air Resources Board compliance sales in North America. This is up from $142 million in Q3 last year, reflecting higher credit generation from our 128,000 vehicle deliveries, all qualifying under stringent EV mandates.

Key drivers of this margin expansion include battery cost deflation, which accounted for roughly 60% of the year-over-year improvement. Our average battery pack cost per kWh fell to $92, down 22% year-over-year from $118, thanks to accelerated adoption of LFP chemistry across our Aether 2 platform—now 65% of production versus 35% a year ago—and the ramp of our in-house 46-series cylindrical cells at Gigafactory Nevada. These cells deliver 15% higher energy density at 12% lower cost than our prior 2170 packs, sourced previously from Panasonic and LG. We've also locked in multi-year offtake agreements for lithium hydroxide at sub-$12,000 per metric ton, mitigating the 30% spot price volatility we've seen this year from Australian and South American suppliers.

Manufacturing efficiencies provided the second major boost. Fixed cost leverage from 42% year-over-year delivery growth—128,000 units versus 90,000 last year—combined with overall equipment effectiveness improvements to 92% across our Fremont and Berlin plants, shaved 3.2 percentage points off COGS as a percentage of revenue. Initiatives like our AI-optimized stamping lines and robotic weld density increases—now 1,200 welds per vehicle on the Aether S sedan—have reduced body-in-white costs by 18%. We're also realizing early benefits from our Shanghai Gigafactory Phase 2, where localization of 85% of components has cut import duties and logistics by 14%.

Third, a favorable mix shift played a role. Premium trims like the Aether X SUV and Performance variants grew to 28% of volume, up from 22% year-over-year, contributing their characteristic 28-32% segment margins versus 18% for base models. Conversely, we've de-emphasized entry-level Aether 1 sedans in favor of higher-margin crossovers, aligning with consumer demand for longer-range vehicles exceeding 450 miles EPA amid range anxiety concerns.

Regionally, performance varied but trended positively overall. In North America, which is 62% of revenue, gross margin stood at 25.4%, boosted by IRA Section 30D incentives effectively reducing our net ASP by $7,200 per vehicle while preserving margins through upstream battery production credits under 45X. Production localization at our new Spartanburg, South Carolina facility—now at 25,000 units run rate—has minimized tariff exposure on Mexican-sourced parts. Europe, at 28% of revenue, saw margins at 19.8%, pressured by 12% year-over-year demand softness due to subsidy phase-outs in Germany and softening used EV residuals, plus aggressive pricing from BYD's Seagull and Seal models. However, our Berlin plant's 4680 cell integration and vertical integration—95% EU-sourced battery materials—offset this, delivering 300 basis points quarter-over-quarter gains. EU tariffs on Chinese imports, now at 45% provisional duties, are a tailwind as we capture share from imported rivals. In China and Asia-Pacific, 10% of revenue, margins held steady at 17.5% despite fierce competition from BYD's Blade Battery ecosystem and NIO's battery-swapping network. Our Shanghai output mix skewed toward export-oriented premium builds, and partnerships with CATL for semi-solid-state prototypes position us for next-gen cost leadership.

Strategically, these trends underscore our multi-year roadmap to sustainable 28-30% automotive gross margins by 2026. We're investing $2.8 billion in CapEx this year—40% on battery tech—to launch our next-gen Aether 3 platform, promising 50% pack cost reduction via silicon-anode cells and dry electrode processes, targeting $60 per kWh by 2025. Vertical integration now covers 72% of our bill of materials, up from 55% two years ago, reducing supplier leverage amid ongoing semiconductor shortages, such as our custom SiC inverter chips from Wolfspeed. Additionally, our software stack—featuring Level 3 autonomy on 40% of the fleet—now generates $450 per vehicle in OTA revenue at 85% margins, accretive to overall gross profit.

Looking forward, we expect Q4 gross margins to expand another 150-200 basis points to 25-25.5%, with full-year 2024 landing at 23.2%, well ahead of our initial 20% guide. Risks remain around lithium price spikes or slower-than-expected 4680 ramps, but our $8.5 billion cash position and hedging provide ample buffer. This positions us to outpace peers like Rivian, still in negative margins, and Lucid, sub-10%, while closing the gap to Tesla's 19% automotive excluding credits.

I'd also like to dive deeper into our cost reduction initiatives, which have been a cornerstone of our operational excellence strategy this quarter. In the hyper-competitive automotive and EV sector—where we've seen peers like Tesla pushing battery costs below $100 per kWh and BYD dominating with their LFP blade battery tech at scale—margin expansion isn't optional; it's existential. Our efforts here have delivered tangible results, driving sequential COGS reductions and positioning us for sustained profitability as we ramp production across our gigafactories.

The key pillars start with supply chain optimization and vertical integration, accounting for 45% of total savings. We've accelerated vertical integration, mirroring Tesla's playbook with our in-house 46-series cylindrical cell production, which is now at 20 GWh annual capacity in our Nevada Gigafactory. This has slashed our battery bill of materials by 28% year-over-year, from $132 per kWh in Q2 last year to $95 per kWh this quarter—well ahead of the industry benchmark of $110 per kWh per BloombergNEF. By localizing 85% of our cathode and anode production, we've insulated against the lithium price volatility that spiked 40% earlier this year due to Australian supply constraints. Procurement costs as a percentage of COGS dropped from 62% to 54%, saving $1,850 per vehicle on average. For context, on our flagship Aether S sedan—our volume leader with 85 kWh packs—this translates to a $1.6 million savings per 1,000 units. We've also renegotiated long-term offtake agreements with suppliers like Albemarle and Ganfeng for spodumene concentrate at a blended $1,200 per tonne, 22% below spot prices, locking in predictability amid Red Sea disruptions.

Manufacturing efficiencies and automation contributed 30% of savings. Our Factory 2.0 upgrades, including AI-driven robotic welding and vision systems from partners like Fanuc, have boosted throughput by 35% while cutting direct labor costs 18%. Scrap rates on structural packs are down to 1.2% from 4.5%, directly feeding into our 62% gross margin on the Aether S, up from 48% a year ago. Capex efficiency is another win: We've reduced structural Capex per GWh of battery capacity from $120 million to $85 million through modular cell-to-pack designs, inspired by CATL's condensed battery tech but optimized for NMC 811 chemistries. This quarter, factory utilization hit 92% across our U.S. and Mexico plants, generating $250 million in fixed cost absorption—critical as we scale to 500,000 units annually by fiscal 2025.

R&D and overhead rationalization accounted for 15% of savings. We've streamlined SG&A by 12% through zero-based budgeting, exiting non-core projects like legacy ICE platform maintenance and consolidating our engineering footprint into three global hubs. R&D spend is now 6.5% of revenue—below Ford's 7.2% but laser-focused on next-gen silicon anodes, targeting $70 per kWh by 2026. Workforce optimization via attrition and reskilling yielded $45 million in savings, without impacting safety KPIs; our lost time incident rate remains at 0.8, industry-leading.

Product design and mix optimization rounded out 10% of savings. By prioritizing high-margin SKUs, we've shifted mix toward our LFP-equipped Aether Lite SUV, which boasts a 22% lower bill of materials than NMC rivals. ASP held steady at $48,500 despite 5% price compression from Tesla's Model Y cuts, thanks to premium features like 800V architecture enabling 10-minute DC fast charging.

Overall, these initiatives delivered a 17% year-over-year COGS reduction per vehicle, from $36,200 to $30,000, outpacing GM's 14% EV cost cuts reported last quarter. Total program savings: $1.2 billion this fiscal year, contributing to EBITDA margins expanding 420 basis points to 8.2%. Sequentially, Q3 COGS fell another 4%, driven by scale—our run-rate production is now 120,000 units per month, unlocking economies that reduce variable costs by $400 per doubling of volume, per our learning curve analysis. Trend-wise, we're tracking ahead of the IHS Markit EV cost parity curve, which projects ICE parity by 2026; we're there now for our base models in key markets. Compared to peers: Our battery costs are 15% below Rivian's, 8% above Lucid's luxury packs but with 2x volume leverage.

Regionally, North America at 65% of production benefited from IRA-compliant sourcing—100% North American critical minerals—unlocking $7,500 per vehicle in credits, amplifying our 22% gross margins. Mexico's nearshoring via our Monterrey plant cut logistics costs 11% amid UAW strikes, positioning us ahead of Detroit Three delays. Europe at 20% saw EU tariffs on Chinese cells up to 38% favoring our localized Gigafactory Berlin ramp, but Red Sea issues inflated ocean freight 25%; we've mitigated with air bridges for high-value packs, holding EMEA COGS flat year-over-year. Volume licensing agreements with Volkswagen Group for joint cell procurement saved another 9%. Asia at 15% faced intense pressure from BYD's $9,500 Seagull, but our Shanghai JV with CATL yields LFP packs at $82 per kWh—10% below local averages. Subsidies in China offset, but we're gaining share via exports to ASEAN. Challenges persist: Nickel surcharges from Indonesia added $120 per kWh temporarily, but hedging covers 70% exposure.

These aren't one-offs; they're embedded in our Margin Momentum framework, targeting 25% gross margins by fiscal 2026 via 1 TWh battery scale. We're deploying GenAI for predictive bill of materials optimization, piloting with a 5% scrap reduction already. Risks like raw material inflation—lithium at $15k per tonne forecast—are hedged 18 months out. In summary, our cost initiatives have de-risked the business, funding $2.5 billion in growth Capex without dilution. This quarter's results validate our path: profitability inflection in Q4, free cash flow positive by mid-2025. We're not just cutting costs; we're building a fortress in the EV wars.

Before handing off, a quick note on forward guidance. Looking ahead to Q4 2024, we are guiding revenue to $16.5 billion to $17.5 billion, representing 15% to 22% sequential growth from Q3 and approximately 25% to 32% year-over-year growth. This guidance assumes vehicle deliveries of 145,000 to 155,000 units, with an ASP of around $48,000, up modestly from Q3 due to favorable regional mix and a shift toward higher-content variants like the Aether X Long Range AWD. Automotive revenues would be $15.2 billion to $16.0 billion, fueled by fully electric models. Regulatory credits are expected to contribute $450 million to $550 million. Energy and services add $1.0 billion to $1.2 billion from Megapack deployments and charging networks.

For full fiscal 2025, we are introducing revenue guidance of $125 billion to $135 billion, implying 25% to 35% growth over fiscal 2024's projected $102 billion. This is predicated on 2.4 million to 2.6 million vehicle deliveries, with ASPs stabilizing at $47,000 to $49,000 amid a richer product mix. Strategic drivers include full-year production of new pickups targeting 250,000 units, launch of a $35,000 compact EV, and initial autonomous fleet deliveries. Battery costs drop another 25% via dry electrode and silicon anodes, targeting under $60 per kWh. Capex of $12 billion focuses on expansions in Texas and India. Vehicle gross margins to 23-25% by year-end, EBITDA at 18%. Risks include semis shortages and policy shifts, but our cash position provides flexibility.

On deliveries for Q1 2025 specifically, we're guiding 450,000 to 480,000 vehicles, 22% year-over-year growth. By model: Aether Prime SUV at 180,000-195,000 units, our volume leader with strong regional demand; Aether Beam Sedan at 135,000-145,000; CyberHauler Pickup at 90,000-100,000, highest growth; Scout Compact at 45,000-50,000 as ramp begins; and emerging models at 5,000. This mix yields 52 GWh batteries, with balanced regional exposure.

Next, Maria Gonzalez will share updates on our manufacturing operations.

Maria Gonzalez:
Thank you, Sarah. We have made significant investments in our manufacturing facilities to enhance capacity and improve efficiency. Our efforts have resulted in record production volumes and reduced manufacturing costs. Good afternoon, everyone. Before we move on, I'd like to provide a detailed walkthrough of our production volumes and capacity utilization rates, which continue to be the backbone of our operational execution in this hyper-competitive EV landscape. Aether Dynamics has positioned itself as a vertically integrated pure-play EV OEM, with a focus on premium mid-size BEVs and our upcoming CUV platform. Our three gigafactories—Fremont Expansion in California, Spartanburg in South Carolina, and the new Shanghai JV with CATL—give us a diversified footprint to navigate tariffs, subsidies, and regional demand dynamics.

In Q3, we produced 142,000 vehicles globally, marking a 28% year-over-year increase from Q3 2023's 111,000 units and a sequential 12% ramp from Q2's 127,000. Year-to-date through Q3, we're at 385,000 units, putting us on track for full-year guidance of 520,000 to 540,000 vehicles—a 35% growth over 2023's 390,000. This outperformance is driven primarily by our Aether X SUV, which accounted for 68% of output at 96,500 units, fueled by strong U.S. fleet orders and our first exports to Europe. Our Aether S sedan followed at 32,000 units, with initial runs of the next-gen compact crossover adding 13,500 units as we exit the pilot phase.

Our nameplate capacity stands at 650,000 vehicles annually across all sites, with an effective throughput of 720,000 once we factor in multi-shift flexibility and our 4680 cell integration. Q3 global utilization hit 78%, up from 72% in Q2 and a robust 22 percentage point improvement year-over-year. This is ahead of the industry average of ~65% for Western OEMs, per recent MarkLines data, and closing the gap on leaders like Tesla, who reported 85-90% at Giga Texas last quarter.

Breaking it down regionally: U.S. operations—Fremont and Spartanburg—represent 55% of our capacity at 400,000 units per year. Q3 utilization was stellar at 92%, producing 112,000 vehicles. Spartanburg, our newest greenfield site, ramped to 95% on the back of Aether X Model Year 25 lines, benefiting from IRA Section 45X credits—we've already claimed over $450 million year-to-date in advanced manufacturing production tax credits for our LFP and NCM cathode lines. Demand here remains red-hot, with U.S. BEV market share for premium segments holding at 18%, per Cox Automotive, as we capture share from legacy players like GM's Ultium ramp delays.

The China JV in Shanghai, at 250,000 units capacity, utilization was 52% in Q3, outputting 30,000 units—primarily Aether S for domestic sales and ASEAN exports. This is up from 40% in Q2, as we navigate softer NEV demand amid China's post-subsidy cooldown. Wholesale volumes dipped 15% year-over-year per CAAM data, but our vertical integration with CATL—supplying 80% of our LFP packs at $85 per kWh—keeps COGS competitive at 72% gross margin on these builds. We're accelerating automation here with ABB robotics for our structural battery pack assembly, targeting 75% utilization by Q1 2025.

Key trends include supply chain resilience. Early 2024 bottlenecks in semiconductor etch tools and lithium hydroxide constrained us to 65% utilization in Q1. We've mitigated this via dual-sourcing from TSMC and Samsung for our ADAS domain controllers, and locking in 18-month offtake with Albemarle for hydroxide at a blended $18 per kg. Technical initiatives driving efficiency: We've rolled out Gen 3 structural packs with 4680 cells across 40% of Aether X lines, boosting energy density to 180 Wh/kg and cutting weld points by 30%, which has improved throughput by 15% per line. Our Industry 4.0 digital twin at Fremont uses Siemens software for predictive maintenance, reducing downtime to under 2%—a level matching BYD's Shenzhen benchmark.

Strategically, this positions us for the 2030 EV mandates. We're investing $2.2 billion in Capex this year, including a 200,000-unit expansion at Spartanburg for our 800V architecture CUV launching H1 2025, and Shanghai Phase 2 for sodium-ion pilots to derisk cobalt exposure. Utilization is forecasted to climb to 85% globally in Q4 and 92% by fiscal 2025, supporting 25% ASP growth and 18% EBITDA margins as scale kicks in. Compared to peers, we're outpacing Lucid's sub-50% utilization while trailing Tesla's volume but gaining on profitability per unit. U.S. strength offsets Europe headwinds—where soft ADAS regs delayed our 5,000-unit pilot—and China's price wars, but our 20% localization in Shanghai shields us from 100% tariffs. Q4 guidance is 145,000 to 155,000 units, with risks tilted to upside from fleet deals.

After me, we will hear from Dr. Raj Patel regarding our technological advancements.

Dr. Raj Patel:
Thank you. Our R&D team continues to push the boundaries of innovation in battery technology, autonomous driving, and connectivity. We are committed to developing cutting-edge solutions that will shape the future of mobility. Thanks, Sarah, and good afternoon, everyone. At Aether Dynamics, we've made transformative strides in EV range and efficiency, directly fueling our record Q3 deliveries of 28,500 vehicles—up 42% year-over-year—and contributing to our gross margins expanding to 28.7%, the highest in our peer group outside of Tesla.

Across our core lineup—the Aether S sedan, X SUV, and our new budget-friendly Bolt Pro hatchback—we've achieved an average EPA-estimated range uplift of 18% year-over-year. That's the Aether S now hitting 462 miles on a single charge with our 105 kWh pack, up from 395 miles in 2023 models. The X SUV clocks in at 485 miles, leapfrogging competitors like the Tesla Model Y Long Range at 330 miles and the Rivian R1S at 410 miles. Efficiency-wise, we're down to 238 Wh/mi across the fleet—a 12% improvement—translating to real-world MPGe figures north of 140, validated by our 15% surge in customer-reported highway efficiency from telematics data.

These aren't incremental tweaks; they're the result of a multi-pronged technical roadmap we've been executing since our 2022 RangeForge initiative. First, battery architecture. We've scaled production of our next-gen 46-series cylindrical cells—partnering with LG Energy Solution and our in-house gigafactory in Nevada—to deliver 285 Wh/kg energy density, a 22% jump from last-gen NMC 811 chemistries. We're avoiding the hype around LFP for premium packs but incorporating BYD-inspired Blade LFP modules in our Bolt Pro for urban fleets, achieving 180 Wh/kg at 20% lower cost per kWh.

Aerodynamics have been a game-changer. Our X SUV now sports a class-leading drag coefficient of 0.208 Cd—better than the Lucid Air's 0.197—thanks to active grille shutters, underbody paneling, and AI-optimized mirrorless door cams. This alone shaves 8% off consumption at highway speeds. On the powertrain front, our third-gen silicon-carbide inverters and axial-flux motors from Turntide Technologies boost peak efficiency to 98.2%, with regenerative braking recapture hitting 75% in urban cycles—up from 65% last year.

Software is the invisible multiplier. Over-the-air updates via our AetherOS 4.2 have rolled out predictive thermal preconditioning, which uses machine learning to optimize cabin and pack temps based on route data from our 1.2 million connected vehicles. This has delivered a 5-7% range boost in cold weather, critical as we saw a 15% uptick in winter deliveries in the Nordics and Canada. Real-world validation? Our fleet-wide efficiency in sub-32°F conditions improved 11% quarter-over-quarter, narrowing the cold-weather penalty to just 22% versus EPA ratings—far better than the industry average of 30-35% for legacy EVs like the Ford Mustang Mach-E.

Regionally, this is tailored to market realities. In the US, our EPA leadership has driven a 25% share gain in the $60K+ SUV segment, per Cox Automotive data, outpacing Tesla's 8% year-over-year growth. Europe’s WLTP cycle favors our aero and regen advantages, with the Aether X testing at 780 km—beating VW ID.7's 620 km—and supporting our 35% delivery ramp in Germany and the Netherlands amid the €7,500 incentive phase-out. In China, where CLTC ratings rule, our Shanghai-assembled Bolt Pro hits 1,050 km, positioning us against BYD's Qin L at 1,000 km, with exports up 60% to ASEAN markets hungry for sub-$30K efficient commuters.

Strategically, these gains are margin-accretive. Cell-to-pack integration cut our battery BoM by 16% to $92/kWh, enabling us to hold ASPs steady at $48,500 while boosting content per vehicle. Customer NPS jumped to 82 from 74, with range anxiety citations down 40% in surveys—directly correlating to our 22% repeat buyer rate. Looking ahead, Q4 will see 4680 cell pilots from our Panasonic JV, targeting 320 Wh/kg and 500+ mile ranges by H2 2025. We're also investing $450 million in solid-state R&D with QuantumScape, aiming for 400 Wh/kg prototypes in 2026 to redefine parity with ICE trucks.

In short, range and efficiency aren't just specs—they're our moat against Tesla's scale and legacy OEMs' catch-up. This positions Aether for 150,000 annual run-rate by FYE '25, with 30%+ margins.

Following me, Tom Reilly will provide insights into our supply chain management.

Tom Reilly:
Thank you. We have implemented robust supply chain strategies to mitigate risks and ensure the reliable flow of materials. Our focus on diversification and strategic partnerships has strengthened our supply chain resilience. Good afternoon, everyone. As we continue to scale our EV platform—highlighted by the strong demand for our Nexus 400 SUV and Voltara hatchback lineup—today I'd like to provide a detailed update on our supply chain dynamics. We've made meaningful progress against persistent headwinds, but let's dive into the specifics with transparency on where we stand, the impacts, and our robust mitigation playbook.

In Q3, supply chain constraints shaved approximately 12% off our planned vehicle production volume, limiting us to 185,000 units delivered versus our 210,000-unit target. This was primarily driven by three vectors: semiconductor availability, battery raw materials volatility, and logistics bottlenecks. Quantitatively, semis represented a 5% drag, cells and packs another 4%, and freight delays the remaining 3%. Year-to-date, these factors have compressed our automotive gross margins by 220 basis points to 18.4%, largely through elevated COGS from spot pricing and expedited air freight—up 15% quarter-over-quarter.

On semiconductors: The ongoing drought in legacy automotive-grade MCUs and power discretes—exacerbated by the ripple effects from TSMC's Taiwan earthquake in April and ongoing U.S.-China export controls—hit us hard. Our 48V mild-hybrid systems for the Aether X rely on Renesas RH850 cores, where lead times stretched to 52 weeks, up from 20 weeks last year. This bottlenecked 8,000 units in our U.S. and European plants. Globally, automotive chip utilization rates remain sub-85%, per Gartner data, versus the 95% pre-pandemic norm.

Battery materials tell a similar story. Lithium carbonate spot prices surged 25% year-over-year to $28,000 per metric ton amid Andean supply disruptions in Chile and Australia's floods, while nickel LME futures spiked 18% on Indonesian export quotas. Our 100 kWh NMC packs for premium models saw cell pricing pressure, pushing average cell costs to $112 per kWh—still down 8% from Q1 thanks to our hedges, but above our $105 per kWh target. Cobalt stabilized at $18,000 per ton after Glencore's ramp-up, but we're exposed given our 20% reliance on DRC-sourced material.

Regionally, Asia-Pacific remains the epicenter: China's lingering issues and Red Sea shipping disruptions inflated ocean freight rates by 40% to $12,000 per FEU, delaying 15,000 tons of components from CATL and LG Energy Solution. In North America, U.S. IRA compliance added scrutiny, disqualifying 5% of our incoming packs due to foreign entity of concern rules. Europe faced its own pain with EU Battery Regulation passporting requirements, slowing homologation for our Berlin plant by two weeks.

Now, turning to our mitigation strategies—these aren't bandaids; they're structural shifts embedded in our $2.8 billion 2024 capex plan, with 35% allocated to supply chain resilience. We've executed 17 key initiatives since Q4 2023, delivering a 28% reduction in constraint-related downtime year-over-year.

Supplier diversification and dual-sourcing first: We've reduced single-source dependency from 42% to 27% across critical tiers. For semis, we qualified onsemi and Infineon as alternates to Renesas, securing 500,000 units via a $450 million multi-year offtake. On batteries, our portfolio now spans six gigafactory partners: 40% CATL (China), 25% LGES (Korea/U.S.), 20% Panasonic (Nevada/Japan), 10% SK On (Georgia), and emerging 5% slots for India's Reliance New Energy and Europe's Northvolt. This mix cut our China exposure from 55% to 38%, shielding us from tariffs and geopolitics.

Vertical integration and localization next: We're accelerating in-house control. Our Nevada Gigafactory 2—ramping to 50 GWh annually by H2 2025—will produce 60% of our LFP and NMCA cells, leveraging low-cost spodumene from our Australian JV with Albemarle. We've invested $800 million in a U.S. cathode plant with RecycLiCo for NMC 8-series precursors, targeting 80% domestic content to maximize IRA's $45 per kWh credits. In Europe, our Magdeburg site now assembles SiC power modules in-house, slashing inverter chip needs by 30% via our proprietary 1200V platform—mirroring Tesla's efficiencies but tailored for mass-market AWD.

Inventory optimization and risk buffers: Ditching pure JIT, we've built strategic stockpiles to 55 days of supply for semis and cells (up from 32 days), at a $650 million working capital cost offset by 4% inventory turns improvement. We locked 70% of 2025 lithium at $22,000 per ton via forwards with Ganfeng Lithium, insulating against further volatility.

Technical and sustainability initiatives round it out. Innovation is our edge. We've shifted 15% of packs to LFP chemistry—cheaper at $92 per kWh and cobalt-free—sourced from BYD's new Thailand plant, boosting energy density to 180 Wh/kg without rare earths. Recycling pilots with Redwood Materials are recovering 92% of black mass from end-of-life packs, targeting 10 GWh equivalent by 2026. Digitally, our AI-driven SCM platform—powered by Palantir Foundry—predicts disruptions with 88% accuracy, automating 40% of RFQs and cutting lead time variability by 22%.

Looking forward, these efforts position us for inflection. We expect Q4 constraints to ease to 5-7% of production, with full-year 2025 volumes ramping 45% to 850,000 units as Giga Nevada hits 80% utilization. Margins should expand 350 basis points to 22% by year-end, driven by scale and $1.2 billion in IRA/ILUC rebates. Risks persist—monitor U.S. elections for IRA tweaks and Taiwan tensions—but our multi-node strategy de-risks us versus peers like Rivian or legacy OEMs lagging on localization. Supply chain resilience isn't just operational—it's our moat in a fragmented $500 billion battery market growing at 28% CAGR.

Now, I'll hand the call back to Alex for the Q&A session.

Alex Rivera:
Thank you. We will now begin the question and answer session. [Operator Instructions]

Operator:
Thank you. Our first question comes from John Smith with Goldman Sachs. Please go ahead.

Analyst 1:
Thanks, and congrats on a strong quarter. On the revenue guidance for next year, how much does that bake in potential IRA changes post-election?

James Harlan:
Thanks, John. Our $125 billion to $135 billion fiscal 2025 guide assumes continuation of current IRA structures, but with our 80% North American content trajectory, we're resilient to tweaks. We've stress-tested for $3,750 rebate scenarios, which would trim only 2-3% off the midpoint, offset by volume levers like fleet deals. Cash buffer allows flexibility without impacting ramps.

Operator:
Our next question from Emily Chen at Morgan Stanley.

Analyst 2:
Great, thanks. Sarah, can you elaborate on the gross margin bridge for Q4 and how cost initiatives factor in?

Sarah Kline:
Absolutely, Emily. Q4's 25-25.5% guide builds on 150-200 bps expansion from Q3, with 60% from battery deflation to under $90/kWh via LFP scale, 25% from 85% utilization leverage, and 15% from premium mix. Cost program adds another $800 per vehicle savings, fully embedded. Peers' pricing won't erode this given our vertical moat.

Operator:
Next from Mike Rodriguez at JPMorgan.

Analyst 3:
